Exercise A

The Long Walk to Freedom

Read the text about Nelson Mandela. Choose the correct word for each gap.

Before you read — optional, not marked
This is just to get you thinking — you can leave it empty and it does not count towards your score.
Reading Text

Nelson Mandela was born in 1918 in a small village in the south-east of South Africa. At that time the country lived under a system called 1. It separated people by the colour of their 2: black families had worse schools, worse hospitals and no vote.

Mandela studied law and became a 3 in Johannesburg. He joined the ANC, a political party which fought against the system. In 1964 a court sent him to 4 for life.

He spent 27 years behind bars, most of them on Robben Island, where prisoners had to break stones in the hot 5. His letters were read by the guards, and for years he was allowed only one visitor every six months.

All over the world, musicians, students and governments demanded his 6. Finally, in February 1990, President de Klerk let him go.

Four years later South Africa held its first free 7, and Mandela became president. He did not want revenge. He wanted a country in which every group had the same 8 — the “Rainbow Nation”.

Exercise B

Relative Clauses: who, which, whose, where, when

Use who for people, which for things, whose for possession, where for places and when for time. After a comma (non-defining clause) you must use which, never that.

Complete the Sentence

1. Nelson Mandela was a man never gave up.

2. Apartheid was a system separated people by colour.

3. Robben Island is the place Mandela spent 18 years.

4. 1994 was the year South Africa held its first free election.

5. He met families homes had been destroyed.

6. The party he joined in 1944 was the ANC.

7. Cape Town, lies in the south-west, is a popular city with tourists.

8. Do you know the journalist interviewed Mandela in 1990?

Exercise D

Writing: A Person I Admire

Write 6–8 sentences about a person you admire — Mandela or somebody else. Use at least three relative clauses.

Think about these questions

• Who is the person, and where does / did he or she live?

• What did this person do that was difficult or brave?

• Why do you admire him or her?

• What could other people learn from this person?

You can use these: a woman who... a man whose... the country where... the year when... ..., which is... fight for give up be proud of
Your text
Aim for 6–8 sentences with at least three relative clauses.
